note: Fixtures for the promoted representation contract (0.4.1-draft). `validator` says which check a row is evidence for: `schema` rows are validated by the schema and must fail AT THEIR INTENDED GATE (expected_schema_path_contains plus expected_instance_path_contains together, because ajv reports schemaPath relative to the innermost $ref and the same string names two gates). `reference` and `semantic` rows are validated by the resolvers in src/representation/validation/, and every one of their negatives is ALSO asserted to be schema-valid -- which is the whole argument for B3: D-1, D-2, D-3 and D-7 all passed a schema. rule_id binds every row to a REP-* invariant, checked in BOTH directions (BP-6): no declared rule without a positive and a negative, no fixture naming a rule that is not declared. D-5 is what a one-way check misses. A row whose `validator` is `evidence` has no fixture file of its own: its evidence is a named test running a production check against the real promoted corpus, and `covered_by` names that test. The coverage check verifies the named test actually exists, so a declaration cannot outlive the test it points at.

fixtures.purpose: The smallest contract the schema accepts. Synthetic throughout: it describes no real design system and carries no real identifier.
BP-3: a 1.0.0 version string requires ready_for_production and zero blockers, so it cannot be used to dress an unapproved contract as approved.
A -draft version permits only not_ready or validation_ready. This is the gate that keeps the -draft suffix honest.
D-5 orphan CV-4: approval must not coexist with open blockers. The research fixture set asserted this rule id against a rule the contract never declared.
D-5 orphan CV-9 / C-1: only a matrix representation may carry an allocation. D-3 is the consequence of nobody checking which strategy a target actually has.
D-5 orphan CV-19 / C-10: enforcement=observed_only requires uniquenessPolicy not_applicable. A rule nobody enforces cannot also claim uniqueness.
D-1 class: a finding with no structured target is a claim nothing can resolve.
D-2 and D-7 class: a blocker whose subject and cited artifact live only in prose.
D-2 had a knownLimitations twin asserting a fact the corpus contradicted. An unanchored limitation cannot be checked against what it describes.
requiredStrategy is meaningful only for a layout_representation target; permitting it elsewhere would make kind-compatibility unenforceable.
D-7 exactly: a blocker citing an artifact. An unpinned path can resolve to different bytes than the ones the claim was made over, so the pin is required, not optional.
The target field is where prose is not allowed. A contract target takes the literal "self".
D-1 is a reference smuggled into a sentence. The narrative object is closed so a new reference cannot be added there instead of to target.
authoringMode is the discriminator that makes "legacy states are migration-only" enforceable without version-sniffing.

REP-01 in the passing direction: the only shape in which a 1.0.0 version string is a true statement. Without this the rule is only ever evidenced by rejection, which cannot show it is satisfiable at all.
REP-02 permits both draft readiness values, and not_ready is the one the baseline does not exercise.
REP-03 in the passing direction: approval is reachable, and what it costs is zero blockers and a confirmation reference.
REP-04 is an if-and-only-if. The negative shows a list carrying an allocation; this shows a matrix carrying one, which is the half a rejection test cannot demonstrate.
REP-05 in the passing direction: an enforced naming rule may claim uniqueness.

REP-06 across all three sites at once, each naming a different collection. A positive that only repeated the baseline would prove the rule is satisfiable but not that it is satisfiable by more than one kind.
REP-07 in the passing direction, and the exact shape D-3 should have had: a rule guarding a matrix says requiredStrategy matrix, and its target resolves to a matrix.

REP-08 in the passing direction: an artifact target carries a content pin. The path is deliberately NOT a real repository file — audit cycle 2 found this fixture naming a tracked file beside a fabricated hash, in a fixture set whose subject is unpinned artifact references. Whether a pin matches the bytes is REP-13, in the reference fixtures, where a reader supplies both.

REP-09 in the passing direction, deliberately mentioning three real ids inside the prose. That is allowed and inert: the narrative is closed, so those ids cannot become references, which is exactly what D-1 needed and did not have.
REP-10 is a two-sided discriminator. The negative shows authored refusing a report; this shows migrated requiring one.
D-1 and D-2 class: a target naming a component set the contract does not contain. The schema accepts it, because a string that matches no pattern rule is just a string.
REP-11 in the passing direction, across two collections.
D-3 reproduced: a rule guarding matrix cells whose target resolves to a list representation. LR-1 exists, so existence checking alone passes this — which is why the research suite did.
The shape D-3 should have had.
D-7 exactly: a blocker citing an artifact that is not there. The reader is present and empty, which is the difference between "checked and absent" and "never checked".
The artifact exists and is the wrong bytes. A path that resolves is not the same claim as a path whose content backs the statement made over it.
No reader supplied. This must fail rather than skip: an unchecked reference reading as a passing one is how D-7 survived a green suite in the first place.
REP-13 in the passing direction: present, and the bytes are the ones the claim was made over.
The pointer is well-formed and resolves to nothing. An index past the end of an array is the silent-miss case, because it looks exactly like a valid one.
REP-14 in the passing direction.
C-3 separated scope from corroboration so a finding could say what it applies to. An unresolvable scope says nothing, at full confidence.
REP-15 in the passing direction, across two scope types.
Two component sets sharing one id. The schema has no uniqueness keyword that reaches this, so it passes there.
C-11 makes buildFrameId a many-to-one reference rather than an identity. A collision makes one string mean two different things depending on which field read it.
REP-16 in the passing direction, with a build frame reference present rather than absent — a null buildFrameId would not exercise the collision check at all.
A schema variant no layout representation covers, and no statement that this is so. Being undocumented is fine; being silently undocumented is what D-1, D-2, D-7 and D-9 all rely on.
REP-17 in the passing direction: the absence is stated.
The other direction: a variant declared undocumented while a representation covers it. A one-way check sees neither this nor the case above.

fixtures.covered_by: the same catalogue with one token inside a sentence is rejected
fixtures.purpose: The negative is a condition carrying a retired token inside a sentence — where D-1 lived and where whole-leaf equality cannot see it. Paired with its clean twin so the two differ in one token.

fixtures.covered_by: a rule catalogue whose conditions are written in live vocabulary passes
fixtures.purpose: The passing direction, over a field a validator interprets. It used to point at the production schema, which is not a contract and which contains a retired token in its own prose — the declared positive evidence was a document violating the rule.

fixtures.covered_by: D-6 — the shared-build-frame probe is byte-identical to its subject
fixtures.purpose: The negative is the real probe set, hashed. A synthetic pair would show the comparison runs, not that the corpus needed it.
The passing direction, so the rule is shown to be satisfiable rather than only violable.

fixtures.covered_by: D-11 — the change plan declares two contradictory statuses
fixtures.purpose: The negative is the real change plan, whose first eight lines carry both statuses.

fixtures.covered_by: a single clear status declaration is accepted
fixtures.purpose: The passing direction, plus a body mention that must NOT count as a second declaration.

fixtures.covered_by: D-9 — the analysis document omits a blocker the contract carries
fixtures.purpose: The negative is the real analysis document against the real contract: ten rows against eleven blockers.

fixtures.covered_by: an enumeration that matches the artifact is accepted
fixtures.purpose: The passing direction, and its mirror — a table listing a member the artifact dropped — is covered beside it.
REP-03 has two clauses and only the blockers one was covered. Approval also costs a resolvable confirmation reference, and a rule-id-level coverage check cannot see a rule half-tested.
The converse gate, enforced by the schema and declared by no rule until audit cycle 2 found it. Declaring ready_for_production requires the version and the approval that earn it.
REP-22 in the passing direction: ready_for_production is reachable, and what it costs is a 1.0.0 version, approval and zero blockers.
